Memory Jogger.new: During the Great Depression, Minnesota let courts temporarily extend mortgage-redemption periods if the mortgagor paid a court-set rental value; a 5--4 Court upheld the law, holding that the Contracts Clause is not absolute and yields to a State's reasonable, temporary, conditioned exercise of its police power in an emergency (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/290/398/}{Justia}).

Judicial Votes.new: The Supreme Court \textbf{affirmed} the judgment of the Supreme Court of Minnesota by a \textbf{5--4} vote. The case was argued on November 8--9, 1933, and decided on January 8, 1934 (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/290/398/}{Justia}; \href{https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/290/398}{Cornell LII}):

Analysis of Opinions.new: \subsubsection{The Five-Factor Balancing Test Applied to Minnesota's Act}
\item \textbf{Burger Court Revival and the \textit{Energy Reserves} Test:}

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Same-Side (Law Upheld): A Temporary, Compensated Pandemic Foreclosure Pause.} During a declared public-health emergency that causes mass layoffs, State W authorizes its courts, on a homeowner's showing of pandemic-related job loss, to postpone a foreclosure sale for up to twelve months, on condition that the homeowner pay the property's court-determined fair rental value toward taxes, insurance, and interest. The law expires when the emergency ends, and the debt, interest, and lender's lien remain intact. Every \textit{Blaisdell} factor favors the State: a genuine emergency, a public rather than private purpose, individualized judicial relief on reasonable conditions, protection of the lender's core investment, and temporary operation. Under the \textit{Energy Reserves} framework that grew out of \textit{Blaisdell}, the measure is a reasonable and appropriate means to a significant public purpose (\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/290/398/}{Justia}).
\item \textbf{Same-Side (Law Upheld): A Notice Rule in a Regulated Industry.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: State Z requires solar lessors in a heavily regulated market to mail a one-page notice before automatic 10-year renewals take effect. \emph{Analysis:} Fails at \emph{Sveen} step one---heavy prior regulation lowers expectations (\emph{Energy Reserves}), and minimal paperwork preserves the core bargain.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Law Struck Down): Permanent Commercial Rent Forgiveness.}

Examples: Future Applications.src: After a hurricane, State X permanently cancels 100\% of six months' commercial rent and personal guaranties without requiring tenant hardship or compensating landlords. \emph{Analysis:} Fails \emph{Sveen}/\emph{Blaisdell}---substantial impairment destroying core lease terms, and permanent, uncompensated relief mirrors \emph{Kavanaugh} and \emph{Melendez}.

Examples: Future Applications.new: \item \textbf{Opposite-Side (Law Struck Down): An Unconditional Five-Year Redemption Extension.} Facing falling farm prices but no acute crisis, State V extends the redemption period on every existing mortgage foreclosure by five years. Mortgagors need not show hardship or pay rent, no court supervises the extension, and the law has no expiration date. The law lacks each of the guardrails that saved Minnesota's statute: it is not tailored to an emergency, offers no individualized relief, leaves the mortgagee-purchaser uncompensated for lost possession, and is not temporary. That is the pattern struck down in \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/295/56/}{\emph{W.\ B.\ Worthen Co.\ v.\ Kavanaugh}, 295 U.S.\ 56 (1935)}, and in the nineteenth-century cases \textit{Blaisdell} distinguished, such as \emph{Bronson v.\ Kinzie}.

Examples: Future Applications.src: To close a budget deficit without raising taxes, State Y permanently repeals a statutory 3\% annual COLA for already-retired teachers. \emph{Analysis:} Public contract triggers \emph{U.S.\ Trust} heightened scrutiny; because less drastic fiscal alternatives exist, retroactive repeal is likely neither necessary nor reasonable.

Examples: Future Applications.new: The result is genuinely uncertain, however, because a court must first decide whether the COLA statute created a contract at all: statutes are presumed not to create contractual rights unless the legislature clearly intended to bind itself, \textit{National Railroad Passenger Corp.\ v.\ Atchison, Topeka \& Santa Fe Railway Co.}, 470 U.S.\ 451 (1985). If no contract exists, the Contracts Clause challenge fails at the threshold.

Key Quotations.src: ``Emergency does not create power. Emergency does not increase granted power or remove or diminish the restrictions imposed upon power granted or reserved. The Constitution was adopted in a period of grave emergency. Its grants of power to the federal government and its limitations of the power of the States were determined in the light of emergency, and they are not altered by emergency. \ldots\ While emergency does not create power, emergency may furnish the occasion for the exercise of power.''
``is not an absolute one, and is not to be read with literal exactness, like a mathematical formula.''

(\href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/290/398/}{Justia}; quoted in \emph{City of El Paso v. Simmons}, 379 U.S.\ 497, 508 (1965), \href{https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/379/497/}{Justia})
``The reserved power cannot be construed so as to destroy the limitation, nor is the limitation to be construed to destroy the reserved power in its essential aspects.''

``If by the statement that what the Constitution meant at the time of its adoption it means to-day, it is intended to say that the great clauses of the Constitution must be confined to the interpretation which the framers, with the conditions and outlook of their time, would have placed upon them, the statement carries its own refutation. \ldots\ With a growing recognition of public needs and the relation of individual right to public security, the court has sought to prevent the perversion of the clause through its use as an instrument to throttle the capacity of the States to protect their fundamental interests.''

``The only legitimate inquiry we can make is whether it is constitutional. If it is not, its virtues, if it have any, cannot save it; if it is, its faults cannot be invoked to accomplish its destruction. If the provisions of the Constitution be not upheld when they pinch, as well as when they comfort, they may as well be abandoned.''
